c.tagline: Cradle of the Revolution — son and trova, Caribbean heat, and Sierra Maestra views.

taxi.fareNote: There is no Uber or ride-hailing in Cuba. Get around by state Cubataxi, shared fixed-route almendrones (classic American cars) and colectivos, or private taxis, always agreeing the fare before you set off. Fares for visitors are often quoted in USD cash; the informal dollar rate far exceeds the official peg, so carry small bills.

emergency.note: 106 reaches the police and 104 the ambulance service; response can be slow, and most casas and hotels will help arrange private medical care for visitors.

hood_landmark.Tivoli: Padre Pico staircase, Santiago de Cuba

avoid.reason: Persistent jinetero hustlers, bag-snatching and overcharging around Parque Céspedes and on dark streets at night.

hood_desc: The colonial core around Parque Cespedes, with the cathedral, Casa de Diego Velazquez and Hotel Casa Granda; the most walkable base for sights, live music and street life.
Santiago's oldest quarter, climbing the hills above the bay via the Padre Pico staircase, with French-Haitian heritage and a claim as the birthplace of trova and son; atmospheric and bohemian.
A leafy district of 1920s neoclassical mansions southeast of the centre, home to embassies, museums and the Melia Santiago; quieter and more upscale.
A calm residential area near the Moncada Barracks and the Plaza de la Revolucion, with a local feel and budget casas particulares.

water.note: Drink bottled or boiled/filtered water; supply and quality are unreliable.

transit.hours: Buses run roughly 5:00-22:00 with a sharp evening drop-off; after dark, private taxis and classic cars are the main option.
transit.note: There is no metro, tram or urban rail; Santiago's hilly historic core is best explored on foot, with taxis for longer hops out to Vista Alegre or the Castillo del Morro.
transit.pay: City buses (guaguas) take a few pesos CUP in cash on board, but they are crowded and unreliable because of fuel shortages; most visitors use shared almendrones on fixed routes, private taxis or bicitaxis, agreeing the fare in cash beforehand.

landmarks: Castillo del Morro (San Pedro de la Roca)
A UNESCO-listed 17th-century clifftop fortress guarding the bay's narrow mouth, with cannon-firing ceremonies and sweeping Caribbean sunsets.
Parque Céspedes
The intense heart of Cuba's most Caribbean city, where the cathedral, Casa Velázquez and town hall witness constant music and street life.
Cementerio Santa Ifigenia
José Martí's grand mausoleum and Fidel Castro's simple boulder tomb make this palm-shaded cemetery Cuba's pantheon of heroes.
Basílica del Cobre
Cuba's holiest shrine rises in the hills nearby, sheltering the tiny Virgen de la Caridad, the island's beloved patroness.
Casa de Diego Velázquez
Reputedly the oldest house in Cuba, this 1520s Andalusian-style mansion of the conquistador governor now displays colonial furnishings.
Cuartel Moncada
Bullet holes still scar the barracks Fidel Castro attacked in 1953, the audacious raid that ignited the Cuban Revolution, now a museum.
Catedral de Nuestra Señora de la Asunción
Rebuilt five times since 1522 against earthquakes and pirates, the cream-coloured basilica presides over Parque Céspedes with twin towers.
Casa de la Trova
The hallowed music house where son cubano legends have played for a century, still delivering Cuba's best live traditional sessions nightly.
Padre Pico Steps & Tivolí Quarter
A famous street staircase climbs into the old French-Haitian quarter, birthplace of revolutionary conspiracies and carnival traditions.
La Gran Piedra
A 63,000-tonne volcanic boulder perched at 1,225 metres in the Sierra Maestra, reached by 452 steps for immense coastal panoramas.

dom.op: Ferrocarriles de Cuba (Union de Ferrocarriles de Cuba) — tickets at the Estacion de Ferrocarriles ticket office

train.note: Santiago's station is on the Alameda near the port, on the outskirts of the centre, so take a taxi or bicitaxi to your casa. The flagship Tren Frances leaves Havana in the early evening and arrives the next morning, running roughly every third day, with an alternative cheaper express on the alternate cycle and daytime services to Camaguey and Santa Clara. Delays of many hours are routine even on the Tren Frances, and cancellations are common - confirm the day before at the ticket office. There are no international trains in Cuba, and the overnight coach is usually faster and more dependable than the train.

bus.note: Cuba is an island, so there are no cross-border coaches. Viazul tourist coaches use a terminal on Avenida de los Libertadores near the train station, with about four daily departures to Havana (12-15 hours, the overnight express being fastest) plus services to Baracoa via Guantanamo (5 hours), Trinidad, Camaguey and Varadero. The Astrobus terminal used mainly by Cubans is well out of the centre and rarely sells to foreigners. Buy Viazul tickets at the counter a day ahead in season; Conectando shuttles and shared taxis colectivos to Havana and Bayamo are alternatives arranged through agencies and casas.

intl.op: Santiago de Cuba bay ferry service — tickets at the pier

ferry.note: Small passenger launches cross Santiago Bay several times a day from the Punta Gorda and Ciudamar landings to the island village of Cayo Granma and to Cayo Smith, a 15-minute hop that doubles as the locals' commute and the cheapest harbour cruise in Cuba. Sailings are weather-dependent and stop early in the evening. Santiago is a major cargo port but has no scheduled international passenger sailings - Cuba has no passenger ferry links to any other country.

half.name: Guantánamo
